title: Pick the right matcher
brief:
The cart holds one Blue Top at Rs. 500. The locators are written for you; the matchers are not.

Replace each `REPLACE_ME(...)` with the matcher that says what the comment above it means. One of them is a trap: read what the element actually contains before you choose.
starter:
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_the_cart_shows_one_blue_top(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://automationexercise.com/view_cart")

    # There is exactly one row in the cart table.
    expect(page.locator("#cart_info_table tbody tr")).REPLACE_ME(1)

    # The quantity cell says exactly "1".
    expect(page.locator(".cart_quantity")).REPLACE_ME("1")

    # The price cell mentions rupees somewhere in it.
    expect(page.locator(".cart_price")).REPLACE_ME("Rs.")

    # The checkout link can be clicked.
    expect(page.get_by_role("link", name="Proceed To Checkout")).REPLACE_ME()
solution:
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_the_cart_shows_one_blue_top(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://automationexercise.com/view_cart")

    expect(page.locator("#cart_info_table tbody tr")).to_have_count(1)
    expect(page.locator(".cart_quantity")).to_have_text("1")
    expect(page.locator(".cart_price")).to_contain_text("Rs.")
    expect(page.get_by_role("link", name="Proceed To Checkout")).to_be_enabled()

checks.name: to_have_count
checks.label: Row count: to_have_count(1)
checks.feedback: "There is exactly one row" is a count. to_have_count(1) is the only matcher that can express it - and unlike counting by hand it retries while the table renders.

checks.name: to_have_text
checks.label: Quantity: to_have_text("1")
checks.feedback: "Says exactly 1" is to_have_text. to_contain_text("1") would also pass here, and would keep passing if the cell said 21 - so it is the weaker check.

checks.name: to_contain_text
checks.label: Price: to_contain_text("Rs.")
checks.feedback: This is the trap. The price cell reads "Rs. 500", so to_have_text("Rs.") fails - it compares the whole string. When you only care about part of the text, to_contain_text is the honest matcher.

checks.name: to_be_enabled
checks.label: Checkout link: to_be_enabled()
checks.feedback: "Can be clicked" is to_be_enabled(). Note it takes no argument - it is a question about the element, not a comparison.

hints.label: Nudge
hints.text: Four matchers, all in the table in the lesson above. The trap is the price: look at what the cell really says.

hints.label: Strategy
hints.text: to_have_count for the rows, to_have_text for the exact quantity, to_contain_text for the price (the cell reads "Rs. 500", not "Rs."), to_be_enabled for the link.

reveal:
The difference between `to_have_text` and `to_contain_text` is where most matcher bugs live.

`to_have_text` is stricter, so prefer it **when you genuinely know the whole string**. When the element also holds a price, a currency symbol or trailing whitespace you do not control, `to_contain_text` says what you mean instead of what you hope.
